# Aggivaccha Sutta (MN 72 (PTS MN i 483))

**ID:** MN 72 (PTS MN i 483)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Aggivaccha Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Vacchagotta on Fire
**PTS:** MN i 483
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn72
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Aggivaccha Sutta* (also known as the *Aggivacchagotta Sutta*, MN 72) records a dialogue between the Buddha and the wanderer (*paribbājaka*) Vacchagotta at the Jetavana monastery [SuttaCentral; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. When Vacchagotta questions him regarding the ten standard unexpounded or speculative metaphysical theses (*avyākata*)—such as whether the world is eternal or finite, and whether the Tathāgata exists after death—the Buddha refuses to take any stance [Li 2012; Ozkan 2013; Rogell 2003]. The Buddha explains that entertaining such speculative dogmas leads only to distress and does not conduce to peace or enlightenment [Li 2012; Galasek 2016]. Instead, having seen the arising and cessation of the five aggregates (*khandha*), the Tathāgata is liberated through non-clinging and has relinquished all imaginings and conceits concerning a self [Sieg 2004; Koller 2016; Wen].

To elucidate the condition of a liberated mind beyond the fourfold tetralemma of existence and non-existence, the Buddha presents the famous simile of an extinguished flame [SuttaCentral; Ozkan 2013]. He asks Vacchagotta where a fire goes when its fuel of grass and wood has burned out; Vacchagotta admits that the question does not apply, as the fire is simply reckoned as extinguished for lack of sustenance [Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. Similarly, the Buddha explains that an awakened being is freed from designation by any of the five aggregates, profound and immeasurable like the great ocean, making assertions of post-mortem rebirth or non-rebirth inapplicable [Kuznetsova et al. 2012].

SuttaCentral notes direct parallels to MN 72 in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 962 and SĀ² 196 / T 100), the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* (Up 3.057), and the Pāli *Abyākata Saṃyutta* (SN 44.1) [SuttaCentral]. Comparative scholarship highlights that while the Pāli sutta frames the unanswered questions across ten positions, the northern parallel in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) expands these into the standard fourteen *avyākṛta* propositions [Li 2012]. DharmaNexus corroborates these textual relationships, calculating major text-reuse links between MN 72 and the *Abyākata Saṃyutta* (SN 44) as well as the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), alongside cross-linguistic alignments with the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99), Śamathadeva's *Upāyikā* (D4094), and Vasubandhu's *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* [DharmaNexus].
